name: Tibetan
notes:
Standard (Lhasa) Tibetan. The spec resolves the Tibetan SYLLABLE, not the letter: spelling is historical, and a syllable is prefix + superscript + ROOT + subscript + vowel + suffix + post-suffix, of which only the root, the vowel and the register survive intact in the modern language.

How each part is expressed:
* The written ONSET is one grapheme key. A superscribed or subjoined letter is a combining mark, so ⟨སྤྲ⟩, ⟨ཁྱ⟩, ⟨ཀྲ⟩ and ⟨ལྷ⟩ are single orthographic stacks that open a single consonant — ⟨ཁྱ⟩ is /cʰ/, ⟨ཁྲ⟩ is /ʈʂʰ/. ⟨གཡ⟩ and ⟨དབ⟩ are the two fixed digraphs of the same kind written with full letters. The inventory is closed and is the onset table of the language, not a product of its parts.
* PREFIXED letters ⟨ག ད བ མ འ⟩ are silent, and being silent carry no inherent vowel either. What they leave behind is aspiration: a prefixed low-register root is the unaspirated member of its pair, so ⟨ག⟩ is kʰà but ⟨དག⟩ is kà. The high-register aspirates keep their aspiration under the same prefixes.
* The TSHEG ⟨་⟩ delimits the syllable. Mapping it keeps every positional and allophonic context syllable-local instead of letting a suffix rule reach across a syllable boundary.
* The RHYME is one unit. A written suffix is not pronounced as itself: it fixes the nucleus, the coda and the tone contour together, so ⟨ད⟩ and ⟨ས⟩ umlaut and lengthen the vowel and leave no consonant (⟨ཁྱོད⟩ [cʰøː]), ⟨ན⟩ nasalises it, ⟨ར⟩ and ⟨ལ⟩ lengthen it, and only ⟨ག ང བ མ⟩ leave a coda. The post-suffix ⟨ས⟩ is never pronounced.
* TONE is a two-way register contrast and it is derivable from the spelling: the written onset decides it. Each register has two contours, flat in an open or sonorant-closed syllable and falling in a syllable closed by a historical stop or by ⟨ས⟩ — which is why ⟨ཁམ⟩ kham and ⟨ཁམས⟩ khams differ only in contour. The contour is written at the end of the rhyme, where the WikiPron gold marks it.

Segments are phonemic, not narrow: the backed and laxed vowels of a closed syllable ([ʌ] for /a/, [ɔ] for /o/) are allophones and are not written, and the prenasalised onsets of the Tournadre transcription are not in the Lhasa phoneme inventory and are not emitted.

KNOWN CEILING. A Tibetan syllable whose first letter is one of the five prefixes is structurally ambiguous: ⟨གང⟩ gang is root + suffix while ⟨དགོན⟩ dgon is prefix + root. Telling them apart needs a syllable parser that reads the whole syllable before choosing, which a left-to-right positional resolution cannot do, so the prefix reading is taken uniformly and the root + suffix spellings are read wrong. The residual error is that, gold rows transcribed narrowly, and — in the WikiPron gold specifically — the rows that give a Classical rather than a Lhasa reading.

DIAGNOSTIC ADDENDUM (bo/wikipron, measured on origin/dev). Recorded here so the next reviewer does not repeat these checks.

U+25CC DOTTED CIRCLE — checked and NOT present. Every dependent-vowel sign in this spec's graphemes table is keyed bare — ི U+0F72, ུ U+0F74, ེ U+0F7A, ོ U+0F7C, ཱ U+0F71, ཻ U+0F7B, ཽ U+0F7D — verified at the codepoint level across graphemes, vowel_graphemes, positional_graphemes and allophones. The dz/my/km/xkz dotted-circle defect class, where a vowel sign is keyed together with the placeholder and so never matches real text, does not extend to this spec.

GOLD COMPOSITION — the headline PER understates real-word difficulty. scripts/gold_composition.py on bo/wikipron gives trivial_share 0.2668 (966 of 3621 raw gold lines are single- or two-character entries covering 91.2% of this spec's declared alphabet, i.e. an alphabet chart folded into the wordlist), trivial_per 0.2103, and real_per 0.4266 against the board headline of 0.3785 (n=1564, real_n=1216). Treat 0.4266 as the number that reflects how this spec does on running words.

TWO TRANSCRIPTION CONVENTIONS IN THE GOLD — the most load-bearing finding, not visible on the board. bod_tibt_broad.tsv mixes two kinds of entry under the same headword: transcriptions prefixed with * are spelling-derived 'reading pronunciations' built syllable by syllable from the letters, ignoring the silent prefixes and suffixes, while unprefixed entries are genuine modern Lhasa transcriptions carrying tone. Across the whole gold, 1227 of 1564 distinct spellings (78.5%) carry two or more transcriptions; restricted to the unprefixed, phonetic-only entries, 374 of 1281 spellings (29.2%) still carry more than one transcription, and inspection of those residual cases shows dialectal and transcription-style variance rather than true minimal pairs — for example ཀ་བ appears as both 'k aː ˥˥' and 'k ɒ w ɒ'. This is evidence that the orthography underdetermines the transcription and that the gold itself is internally inconsistent; it does NOT establish a PER floor, since the harness's oracle scoring (evaluate_words_oracle in scripts/benchmark.py) takes the best-matching reference per spelling, so multiple references make a homograph easier to match, not harder. A gold that mixes reading-pronunciations with real transcriptions is measuring two different things under one row.

SANSKRIT-LOAN GAP — six words in the gold (0.38% of 1564) produce an UNKNOWN token from this spec's own G2P._unmapped_chars: སེངྒེ, སམ་ཊ, ཨོཾ, མོ་ཊ, དྲྭ, བུད་དྷ. The uncovered characters are the retroflex ཊ, the anusvara ཾ, and three-member consonant stacks (subjoined ྒ/ྷ/ྭ in combinations this table does not enumerate) — all Sanskrit transliteration machinery, not native Tibetan orthography. Recorded as a known small gap that needs a sourced account of how Sanskrit loans are transliterated into Tibetan phonology before it is filled; not worth a rushed fix.

STRUCTURAL VERDICT. Written Tibetan preserves an eleventh-century consonant-cluster orthography that modern Lhasa Tibetan realises largely as tone and vowel quality rather than as segments, and the mapping from the historical cluster to its modern reflex is lexically conditioned, not cleanly rule-governed beyond what this spec already encodes (prefix-conditioned register, rhyme-conditioned nucleus and contour). This row plausibly has a ceiling that only a pronunciation lexicon, not further G2P rules, can move. He, Xiangzhen (2018), 'Tibetan Lhasa Dialect Tone Conversion System Design and Implementation', IEEE ICRIS, DOI 10.1109/icris.2018.00085, is a documented route toward a rule-based tone-from-orthography system for whoever picks this up — only its Crossref metadata (title, author, venue, DOI) was retrieved, not the paywalled full text, so no specific rule from it is cited or shipped here. The wikipron gold for this language mixes three transcription conventions in one unlabelled two-column file, and only one of them is Lhasa. Of its 3621 rows, 1538 carry a leading reconstruction asterisk and no tone, 1692 carry Chao tone letters, and 391 carry neither; no row carries both, and the same headword recurs across the groups. They correspond to the three pronunciation kinds en.wiktionary's Module:bo-pron generates for a single entry: an Old Tibetan reading inferred from the spelling, the Lhasa reading, and readings for the non-Lhasa dialects (Batang, Dege, Zekog, Bla-Brang, Arik, Lahuli-Spiti, Gyaitang, Maqu, Aba, Mdung-Nag). Old Tibetan is a distinct historical stage whose phonemic system tracks the letters of the alphabet rather than modern pronunciation (Hill 2010), which is why the asterisked readings look like transliterations of the spelling. Scored in isolation this spec reaches PER 0.2363 on the Lhasa rows, 1.0364 on the asterisked rows and 1.0546 on the dialect rows, so the published row PER of 0.3871 describes the mixture and not this spec. The rows are left in place rather than filtered: the file keeps no per-row label, so the dialect rows cannot be attributed to adx or khg, and no Old Tibetan spec exists to score the asterisked ones against. Read the row as a floor on Lhasa accuracy, and read 0.2363 as the number that describes it.

sources.publisher: Tibetan and Himalayan Library, University of Virginia
sources.notes: The onset table this spec transcribes: every written onset spelling against its Lhasa onset and tone register. Consulted as reproduced in the Wikipedia articles 'THL Simplified Phonetic Transcription' and 'Tibetan pinyin'.

sources.author: Tournadre, Nicolas & Sangda Dorje
sources.title: Manual of Standard Tibetan: Language and Civilization
sources.notes: The standard reference grammar of Standard Tibetan and the source of the eight-vowel analysis and the nasalised series; edition not consulted directly.

sources.title: Lhasa Tibetan
sources.publisher: In: Thurgood, G. & LaPolla, R. (eds.), The Sino-Tibetan Languages, Routledge
sources.notes: The two-tone analysis, and the complementary distribution of the falling contour with a final stop that this spec's contour rule states.

sources.author: SASM/GNC/SRC
sources.title: Transcription of Tibetan (Tibetan pinyin)
sources.publisher: State Administration of Surveying and Mapping, China
sources.notes: Official transcription of Standard Tibetan; its rhyme table, whose Lhasa IPA column follows Brush (1997), is the source of the suffix-conditioned nuclei, and its onset-variation section of the medial ⟨བ⟩ lenition.

sources.author: Brush, Beaumont
sources.title: The Status of Coronal in the Historical Development of Lhasa Tibetan Rhymes
sources.notes: The Lhasa rhyme inventory behind the rhyme table.

sources.author: Zhang, Yubin
sources.title: Central Tibetan (Lhasa)
sources.publisher: Journal of the International Phonetic Association 54(2)
sources.notes: Illustration of the IPA for Lhasa Tibetan: the consonant inventory, which carries no prenasalised series, and the four realisations of /ɹ/.

sources.author: Lee, Jackson L. et al.
sources.title: WikiPron: A Tool for Extracting Pronunciation Data from Wiktionary
sources.notes: Source of the bod_tibt_broad.tsv gold registered in scripts/benchmark.py. Three quarters of its words carry both a Lhasa reading and a Classical one; this spec describes the Lhasa language.

sources.author: Hill, Nathan W.
sources.title: An overview of Old Tibetan synchronic phonology
sources.notes: Old Tibetan is a distinct historical stage with its own phonemic system, correlated with the letters of the Tibetan alphabet rather than with modern Lhasa pronunciation. Cited for the audit record below, which identifies part of the wikipron gold as Old Tibetan readings; this spec describes Lhasa and takes nothing else from it.

ancestors.notes: Sanskrit adstrate: Classical (Buddhist) Tibetan calqued and borrowed massively from Sanskrit.
Chinese adstrate: areal and modern loanwords.

wikipron.measured: bod_tibt_broad.tsv is not one variety. Of its 3621 rows, 1538 (42.5%) carry a leading reconstruction asterisk and no tone, 1692 (46.7%) carry Chao tone letters, and 391 carry neither; no row carries both, and the same headword recurs across conventions (see the citation for hill2010). The three groups are the three pronunciation kinds en.wiktionary's Module:bo-pron generates for one entry: an Old Tibetan reading inferred from the spelling, the Lhasa reading, and the non-Lhasa dialect readings (Batang, Dege, Zekog, Bla-Brang, Arik, Lahuli-Spiti, Gyaitang, Maqu, Aba, Mdung-Nag), which the scrape flattens into a two-column file with the labels discarded. Scored in isolation the spec reaches PER 0.2363 on the 1692 Lhasa rows (n=1258), against 1.0364 on the asterisked Old Tibetan rows and 1.0546 on the unlabelled dialect rows: the latter two are not near-misses on Lhasa but different targets, so the 0.3871 row PER measures the mixture rather than this spec's accuracy. Not an orthography limitation: Lhasa tone is derivable from the written initial, and the spec emits it. Splitting the gold was declined because the file carries no per-row label, so the dialect rows cannot be assigned to the adx or khg specs, and there is no Old Tibetan spec to score the asterisked rows against.
